description: This chart displays the distribution of problem types categorized by difficulty—easy, medium, and hard—based on correctness under two conditions: with knowledge (N+K+) and without knowledge (N−K+), as well as combinations involving reasoning errors (N+K− and N−K−), all evaluated under the CoT (Chain-of-Thought) setting. Each difficulty level is represented by a separate pie chart, with four distinct segments: teal for N+K+ (knowledge and reasoning correct), yellow for N−K+ (no knowledge but reasoning correct), orange for N−K− (no knowledge and reasoning incorrect), and red for N+K− (knowledge but reasoning incorrect). The easy chart shows the largest segment as yellow (N−K+, 45.9%), followed by teal (N+K+, 40.6%), orange (N−K−, 10.1%), and a small red slice (N+K−, 3.3%). The medium chart has the largest segment as yellow (N−K+, 44.3%), followed by teal (N+K+, 44.6%), then red (N+K−, 7.2%), and a small orange slice (N−K−, 3.9%). The hard chart shows the largest segment as orange (N−K−, 36.8%), followed by yellow (N−K+, 36.2%), teal (N+K+, 20.1%), and a small red slice (N+K−, 7.0%). All pie charts include percentage labels within their respective slices and are accompanied by a shared legend on the right that maps the colors to the four categories. The slices are visually arranged in descending order of size within each pie chart, though no slice is visually emphasized or exploded.
caption_used: Problem distribution based on correctness under the w/ knowledge and w/o knowledge settings using CoT. The results indicate that while easier problems are primarily hindered by a lack of knowledge (N−K+ at approximately 50%), medium problems show a consistent dominance of reasoning-based errors (N−K− at 15%). For hard problems, the primary bottleneck lies in the inability to integrate geometric reasoning, as evidenced by the sharp decline in N+K+ to below 10%.
